title: TTL sensitivity and prefetch tuning (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is an exploratory notebook-style writeup for TTL (time-to-live) parameter sensitivity and small-window prefetch tuning on the KV cache. Goal is to find a safe default TTL + prefetch window that improves reuse and reduces paging without increasing p99 tail latency for interactive generation workloads.

Background / motivation:
- Observed increasing paging incidents during peak hours (see ENG-4123). Paging correlates with sudden drops in reuse rate and p95/p99 latency spikes.
- Current default: kv-ttl=60s, prefetch-window=0 (disabled). This was conservative but may be leaving reusable KV entries to be evicted early when load bursts occur.
- Hypothesis: a modest TTL bump plus small prefetch (1-2 tokens ahead of predicted consumption) will increase reuse rate and reduce memory churn, improving unit cost. But larger TTLs can increase memory residency and cause bandwidth saturation. Need to quantify tradeoffs.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Workload: mixed chat/generation toy trace built from production-sampled sessions (sequence length mix: 20% <128, 60% 128-512, 20% >512). 20k requests per minute sustained, 4x bursts for 30s every 10m.
- Hardware: 4x A100 40GB nodes, same runtime image as prod; instrumentation: PMU counters, NVML GPU mem bw, OS-level page fault counters, per-instance telemetry (reuse hits, eviction count, resident bytes).
- Variables:
  * kv-ttl: 30s, 60s (baseline), 120s, 300s
  * prefetch-window: 0 (baseline), 1, 2
  * eviction-policy: lru (baseline), lru+age-bucket (prototype) -- limited runs
- Metrics captured: reuse_rate (per-request avg prefix reuse %), evictions/s, paging_events/min, mem_bw_avg (GB/s), tokens/sec throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, tail spikes during bursts.

Commands / flags used:
- ./run_bench --trace=prod-sample-202509 --clients=200 --kv-ttl=120 --prefetch-window=1 --evict-policy=lru
- Telemetry captured via /metrics endpoints and perf counters (scripts/collect_kv_bench.sh)

Quick summary of results (abridged):
- kv-ttl=30s, prefetch=0 (aggressive eviction): reuse_rate 24%, evictions/s 18k, paging 14/min, p99 latency 690ms (high tail)
- kv-ttl=60s, prefetch=0 (baseline): reuse_rate 33%, evictions/s 12k, paging 9/min, p99 520ms
- kv-ttl=120s, prefetch=0: reuse_rate 41%, evictions/s 8k, paging 5/min, p99 510ms
- kv-ttl=120s, prefetch=1: reuse_rate 48%, evictions/s 6k, paging 3/min, p99 530ms (slight p99 increase under sustained burst due to higher mem bw)
- kv-ttl=300s, prefetch=2: reuse_rate 56%, evictions/s 4k, paging 1/min, p99 760ms (severe tail under 4x bursts; mem_bw_avg 240 GB/s saturated on node -> queueing)

Interpretation / notes:
- TTL increase from 60->120s gives clear reuse improvements and fewer evictions with minimal p99 impact for steady-state load.
- Small prefetch (1) improves reuse further but can increase short-term memory bandwidth pressure during bursts. This shows up as slightly worse p99 under the 4x burst profile, despite fewer paging events. Likely reason: overlapping DRAM reads for prefetched pages + normal demand creates transient bandwidth queueing.
- Very large TTL + larger prefetch (300s + 2) trades off paging for bandwidth saturation and worse tail latency. So naive increases are dangerous.
- Eviction counts are a reasonable proxy for memory churn; paging lags eviction trends (eviction down -> paging down) but bandwidth constraints are orthogonal.

Micro-observations and traces:
- Trace A (kv-ttl=120, prefetch=1): single node NVML showed mem_bw spike to 180 GB/s during 30s bursts (baseline ~110 GB/s). Reuse heatmap indicates hot prefixes held in memory and reused across requests.
- Trace B (kv-ttl=300): sustained elevated resident set per process (+12GB) and per-node mem_bw near saturation (230-250 GB/s), GPU utilization unchanged but host-side CPU busy-wait increased (sys time +8%).
- Page fault backoff observed in system logs when mem_bw saturates; long tail latencies correlate with page fault spikes in the kernel (samples attached in linked_artifacts).

Open questions / TODOs:
- We need a workload-aware TTL: static value is suboptimal. Can we have TTL tied to observed reuse half-life per model/route? (e.g., adaptive TTL that decays based on recent reuse).
- Prefetch throttling: implement a soft limiter that gates prefetch concurrency by current mem_bw utilization or a token-bucket on expected bytes/sec.
- Eviction policy improvements: test age-bucket + reuse-frequency hybrid to avoid evicting warm-but-seldomly-used prefixes during bursts.
- Explore per-tenant memory caps to prevent single noisy customer from saturating mem_bw globally.

Immediate proposed action items (short-term):
- Default change candidate: kv-ttl := 120s, prefetch-window := 0 (safe), ramp in canary; rationale: consistent reuse improvements with minimal p99 regression. Owner: Priya. Target: canary next week.
- Implement simple mem_bw monitor in runtime that reduces aggressive prefetching when node mem_bw > 180 GB/s; prototype PR: serving#987 (Miguel).
- Add a synthetic micro-burst test to CI that reproduces the 4x burst profile so we catch regressions early. Owner: Chen.

Longer-term research items:
- Develop an adaptive-TTL controller that uses EWMA of observed reuse time-series to set TTL per-model/route. Simulate using collected traces (see scripts/ttl_sim.py) before runtime rollout.
- Quantify tenant isolation strategies (cgroups, mem throttling) effect on mem_bw and tail latency.

Notes to self / friction items encountered:
- Perf counters require root on CI nodes. For smaller quick runs, we used NVML + /proc metrics which is noisier. Need a stable method for production-like readings.
- Tracing overhead: enabling detailed KV-hit attribution increases p99 slightly; sampling-level telemetry recommended for live traffic.

Attachments / artifacts to examine (in order):
- perflogs/ttl120_pref1_burst1.trace (heatmap + flame graph)
- graphs/reuse_by_ttl.png (reuse vs ttl)
- tables/evictions_paging_summary.csv

Bottom line (working conclusion):
- Conservative TTL increase to 120s is a low-risk win. Small prefetch improves reuse but must be throttled by a mem_bw-aware mechanism to avoid tail degradations during bursts. Long TTLs without bandwidth safeguards lead to worse p99.

Next meeting: sync with Miguel/Chen/Ravi on 2025-10-06 to lock canary parameters and timeline.

Unresolved decisions to raise at meeting:
- Should default prefetch remain disabled in hosted API while we ship mem_bw-throttle? My current recommendation: yes.
- Prioritize adaptive TTL vs prefetch throttling? I propose throttling first (lower engineering effort) and adaptive TTL as follow-up.

End of doc.

-- Priya
